tr.td: 23 November 1887 (one source says on or about 22 November)
A strike of sugar plantation workers, organised with the Knights of Labor
Not established; estimates run from eight to 300, with DeSantis and some historians favouring 30 to 60
No investigation aimed at bringing anyone to account, only a hasty coroner's inquest; one source says nobody was ever held accountable
An estimated 10,000 workers, most of them black; one source says nearly 1,000 were white
Lafourche, Terrebonne and St. Mary, with Iberia also named by one source
Samuel Douglas McEnery, himself a planter
Judge Taylor Beattie, who led the committee that sealed the town
Eight names on a coroner's inquest report; a priest's journal says a dozen
Jack Conrad, a Union army veteran, shot four times
A 2016 book, a memorial committee and a proposed archaeological survey of a suspected burial site

li.a: 64 Parishes (Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities): Thibodaux Massacre
National Archives, Prologue magazine: Tracing an Atrocity
Associated Press, published by The Advocate: Diverse group honoring victims of 1887 Thibodaux Massacre
Nicholls State University, Garde Voir Ci: The Struggle to Work // The Thibodaux Massacre

content.p: In the cane country of south Louisiana, in the last week of November 1887, a strike by thousands of sugar plantation workers ended in a morning of shooting in the town of Thibodaux. Armed white men went through the black neighbourhood east of the railroad tracks, firing at people in the streets and in their homes. Accounts say the shooting went on for two to three hours. Nobody knows how many died: figures range from eight in an official inquest to as many as 300 in one encyclopedia entry, and the reporter who found the key records, John DeSantis, puts it between 30 and 60.

According to the Associated Press, the only investigation of the incident was not an attempt to bring anyone to account. It was a pension examiner's check on whether a wounded black veteran qualified for a benefit. The strike was crushed, and the sugar workers of Louisiana did not organise on that scale again for decades.

The grievances were old. According to the National Archives account by the reporter John DeSantis, most plantation workers earned 50 to 65 cents a day, and were paid at least partly in scrip: cards or tokens good only at the plantation store, where prices could be inflated. Another writer put a field hand's pay at about 13 dollars a month and said store prices were often marked up 100 percent. A Louisiana law, as 64 Parishes describes it, bound a worker who was in debt to the plantation store to stay and work until the debt was cleared, which that entry says kept freed people in conditions close to the slavery they had left.

The Knights of Labor, an integrated union based in Philadelphia, saw an opening. DeSantis writes that it reached out to plantation teachers, ministers, freemasons and black barbers, people the workers respected. In 1886 it set up Local Assembly 8404 for sugar workers. In October 1887 the union delivered a list of demands to the Louisiana Sugar Planters Association. DeSantis says the demands were composed by a black teacher named Junius Bailey. They asked for an end to scrip, a small wage rise and payment every two weeks. DeSantis, speaking to a Nicholls State University publication, put the wage demand at a dollar a day, or a dollar and a quarter for night work. The planters refused.

The strike began on 1 November, timed for the weeks of the cane harvest, when a crop that was not cut and ground before frost was lost. An estimated 10,000 workers stopped work. Most were black, though one source says nearly 1,000 were white. They also refused to leave the plantation cabins they lived in, and local sheriffs' efforts to evict them did not work, according to libcom.org.

The planters turned to the governor. Samuel Douglas McEnery, who was a planter himself, sent state militia. The National Archives account says the troops arrived from New Orleans on 2 November and were quartered in Thibodaux with a Gatling gun, which was set up in front of the Lafourche Parish courthouse. They fanned out across the plantations, evicted the strikers and protected the replacement workers. The evicted families and workers poured into Thibodaux and crowded into the black part of town.

When the soldiers left, around 18 November according to the National Archives account, tension rose. Accounts say shots had been fired at white strikebreakers; libcom.org places this in Terrebonne Parish and adds that strikers who had been forced off the plantations were believed to have fired into sugar mills. Several accounts describe a town in fear. DeSantis told the Associated Press that the white population of Thibodaux was very afraid, and that the workers had nowhere to go.

A local judge, Taylor Beattie, and other officials backed a vigilance committee at a heated meeting at the town hall, says the National Archives account. Martial law was declared, and volunteer sentries closed the roads into town. 64 Parishes adds that the committee ordered black people to show a pass to enter or leave the town, and that armed committee members shut the entrances on the morning of 22 November, as that entry dates it, which led some strikers to believe they were in danger. DeSantis said the order made the strikers more afraid.

The Thibodaux priest, Charles Menard, wrote in his yearly journal that the strikers were flooding the town and threatening to burn it down. The same fear shows in libcom.org's account of the rumour among white residents. None of the accounts offers evidence that the rumour was true.

In the hours before dawn on Wednesday 23 November, two of the sentries, Henry Gorman and Joseph Molaison, were shot and wounded at the southern end of town, according to the National Archives account. The Associated Press said the two were hit about five minutes apart. Father Menard's journal puts the number of men on the picket at six and says two were seriously wounded.

Who fired is not known. DeSantis told the Associated Press that a black weekly newspaper blamed the vigilantes themselves, while white townspeople blamed the strikers. The shooting of the two sentries was the spark. As Father Menard recorded it, the angry guards ran to the scene and fired on "the group of negroes from whence the shots had come", in his words. DeSantis told the Associated Press that by full light armed mobs were in back-of-town Thibodaux.

The National Archives account says the shooting that followed was not aimed only at strike leaders. A pension examiner, Charles Grannis, summed up what he found in the file of a wounded veteran this way: the regulators went about town "shooting every colored person in sight". DeSantis told the Associated Press that the testimony in that file, which he found in the National Archives, confirms that mobs were pulling people out of houses.

The veteran was Jack Conrad, who had joined the Union army in New Orleans in 1862 and served in the 75th US Colored Troops. In an affidavit, he said he was asleep in his rented house in back-of-town Thibodaux when a noise woke him. He put the mob at 50 or 60 men, all white residents of Thibodaux and the area. When he opened his door, he said, one of them said "crack down on him", and they started shooting. Conrad, his son Grant and his brother-in-law Marcelin Weldon were told to line up and began to run. Grant, then about 19, was shot dead behind a water barrel. Weldon was shot as he ran the other way. Conrad crawled under his house, and the gunmen moved on after taking him for dead. He was hit four times; a doctor's diagram in the file shows the wounds, and shattered bones in his upper body. DeSantis notes that Conrad was not on strike, though the file indicates Grant had left his job in the fields.

Witnesses in the same file included the Rev. Thomas Jefferson Rhodes, pastor of Moses Baptist Church, who described the mass shooting of black residents in an affidavit, and Conrad's daughter, who also saw her father shot. According to the book blurb quoted by Yesterday's America, a future member of the US House of Representatives was among the leaders of a mob that forced black men from their houses to a stretch of railroad track and told them to run before shooting them. The blurb does not name him, and the other accounts do not either.
The counts differ from source to source.

One official tally came from a hasty coroner's inquest. DeSantis says an archivist at Nicholls State University, Clifton Theriot, found its report in a file at the university's library. It dealt mostly with the wounding of the two sentries, concluded that "a riot" had broken out, and listed the names of eight people killed on its first page. Father Menard's journal says a dozen were killed and some wounded. Some Louisiana papers at the time reported 25 strikers dead, DeSantis writes. A New Orleans newspaper, the Pelican, mocked the official reports, and its correspondent wrote of "lame men and blind women shot", according to the National Archives account.

DeSantis, who calls the official eight and the priest's dozen understatements, says historians' estimates of 30 or more, with some as high as 60, are likelier. He told the Associated Press that records are sketchy but point to 30 to 60 dead. The Nicholls State publication reports nearly 60 killed, citing his book. Mary Pugh, a plantation mistress, wrote that white guardsmen began hunting for the leaders and that "every one that was found or any suspicious character was shot", in a passage quoted by 64 Parishes. That entry itself says at least thirty-five and as many as 300 were killed, and calls the number uncertain. A writer for libcom.org gives 30 to 300.

No report ever turned up of white casualties beyond the two sentries, even in newspapers friendly to the suppression of the strike, the National Archives account says. The Shreveport Guards, a militia company, are considered by libcom.org to have taken part in the killing; the other accounts do not mention it.

The strike was over. Workers went back to the plantations. In Menard's telling, the strikers "realizing that they had been tricked and duped" asked for work without conditions, and the grinding went on "in calm and peace". Pugh, in her letters, predicted that the killings would "settle the question of who is to rule" for the next 50 years. The National Archives account and 64 Parishes both say no serious attempt to organise Louisiana's sugar workers was made for more than half a century, until the 1950s by one count; the Nicholls publication says laws by white Democrats kept sugar workers from organising until the 1940s.

According to the Yesterday's America excerpt, nobody was ever held accountable, records disappeared and some of the perpetrators came from well-regarded families in town. DeSantis says the index of official documents at the Lafourche Parish courthouse that would have covered 1887 was missing from its shelves, with no telling how long. An unsigned letter published in a local paper after the killings said it would be "better for all concerned that this page be torn out of our history, rather than try to explain." The National Archives account says the official version, that rioters had converged on the scene of the sentries' shooting, was the prevailing tale for a century afterward.

DeSantis, a reporter at the Times of Houma and Thibodaux, spent more than 20 years looking for proof. Victims' names were absent from the old newspaper accounts, which spoke only of "the negroes." His break came in 2016, when the Nicholls archivist matched names in the coroner's report, and he traced Grant Conrad's family through census records to Jack Conrad's federal pension file. Archives staff told DeSantis that the 1890 Disability Pension Act allowed Civil War veterans to claim for injuries not tied to their service, and that such files are often detailed. A researcher at the African-American Civil War Museum in Washington pulled it. The file held, DeSantis says, the first accounts of the violence from black people who suffered or witnessed it, given in affidavits.

His book on the killings, published by The History Press in 2016, followed. Through it he found Conrad's descendants, among them a retired airman in Thibodaux, Sylvester Jackson, who had not known of his great-grandfather's story. Another descendant, Wiletta Ferdinand, said that the family was grateful and did not feel the past was being dredged up. An American flag was flown over the US Capitol at the request of Representative Cedric Richmond to honour Conrad and the other victims.

Local tradition holds that victims are buried in a mass grave on the grounds of what is now a black American Legion post in Thibodaux. DeSantis learned from elders that the lot had been a burial place for mules and other work animals. In 2017 DeSantis and others set up a memorial committee that aimed to pay for an archaeological survey. Its 19 or 20 members included a descendant of Jack Conrad, at least one descendant of a local plantation family, and Denis Gaubert, local commander of the Sons of Confederate Veterans, who said that most of those killed were probably "innocent of any kind of crime." Mark Rees, who heads a public archaeology lab at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, said a first survey would cost up to $24,000. The plan was to rebury any remains found in consecrated ground. Whether the survey went ahead is not reported in the coverage from that time.
A libation ceremony led by Thomas J. Durant Jr., professor emeritus of African-American studies at Louisiana State University, was held on the site in February 2017.
